I obtain a new unbounded compensation obstruction and a separate obstruction to joint closure through the two existing four-stem cores. I do not yet exclude all finite AA closures, and I have no complete feasible counterexample.The main new conclusions are:A positive source owning the forced bottom point  $p$  forces  $R\ge2$ . The proof finds two distinct original  $A/X$  occurrences on that owner, in addition to the original double’s activation. It applies at arbitrary clearance and does not restrict incoming widths, far heights, source number, or contact graph.The two staircases cannot both terminate their adjacent-wall routes in owners from the other staircase’s four-stem core. At least one terminating owner must lie outside the union of the two cores. This explicitly allows shared owners and checks both original tips.In the branch where  $p$  belongs to a phase01 terminal with predecessor south and bar east, the next forced endpoint cannot belong to either positive double—or to any other positive source.These are structural restrictions on unrestricted closure. The remaining negative-source continuations still lack a well-founded descent.1. A positive bottom owner forces  $R\ge2$ Fix one of the doubles in the given normalization,
$$O=U(6,a,b),$$
with unactivated left terminal, activated right terminal, and incoming phase11 owner
$$L(r,c)=(h+2-r,c+1).$$
Put
$$g=a-h\ge4,\qquad p=(h+3,2).$$
The point  $p$  is an original support of  $O$ . It sees the persistent endpoints
$$(h+3,1)\in E_O,\qquad (h+2,2)\in E_L.$$
Therefore mandatory-support feasibility forces  $p\in P$ .Translate  $p$  to  $(0,0)$ . In these relative coordinates: $O$ ’s original left endpoint wall is column  $-1$ , ending at row  $g-3$ .Its retained beyond-tip support is  $(g-2,-1)$ .Consequently
$$q=(g-2,0)\notin\bigcup_i(E_i\cup T_i).
\tag{1}$$
 $L$ ’s original bar occupies rows  $-2,-1$ , columns  $0,\ldots,v_L-1$ .Let  $F$  be the unique original endpoint owner of  $p$ . It is distinct from  $O$  and  $L$ :  $p$  was an original  $O$  support, and it lies below every original  $L$  endpoint.1.1 The only possible positive roleAt  $p$ , north and west are foreign original endpoints. Thus an original U endpoint there can only be:a terminal with predecessor east or south; oran outer bar corner with its two original endpoint neighbors east and south.The two positive orientations among these are:a terminal with predecessor south and bar west;an outer corner with bar south and stem east.The first is impossible. If its incident height is  $D$ , its near stem contains  $(0,0),\ldots,(D,0)$ . Forbiddenness of  $q$ , together with evenness, gives
$$D\le g-4.$$
But its westward bar in rows  $D-1,D$  then crosses  $O$ ’s original wall in column  $-1$ .Therefore a positive owner at  $p$  must have the second orientation. Its exact relative source map is
$$\boxed{F(r,c)=(c-1,r).}
\tag{2}$$
Its bar is columns  $0,1$ , rows  $0,\ldots,w_F-1$ .1.2 Both original exterior bar-end selections are consumedFirst,
$$\boxed{w_F\le g-4.}
\tag{3}$$
Indeed, if  $w_F\ge g$ , then  $q=(g-2,0)$  is an original  $F$  endpoint. If  $w_F=g-2$ , then  $q$  is exactly an original  $F$  support: its far exterior bar-end selection. Both contradict (1). These cases exhaust the alternatives because  $w_F$  and  $g$  are even.Now inspect the two original exterior bar-end selections of  $F$ . These are precisely the  $j=0$  selections included in the definition of  $X$ .The near one is
$$s_{\mathrm{near}}=(-1,0).$$
It is already an original endpoint of  $L$ , so it is consumed.The far one is
$$s_{\mathrm{far}}=(w_F,0).$$
It has its persistent original  $F$  anchor
$$(w_F-1,0)\in E_F.$$
By (3), it also neighbors
$$(w_F,-1)\in E_O.$$
Thus it sees two distinct persistent endpoints and cannot remain selected:
$$s_{\mathrm{far}}\in P.
\tag{4}$$
This second contact can also be viewed directly as a shared mandatory support. Since  $w_F$  is even and  $w_F\le g-4$ , the point  $(w_F,0)$  is an original interior support of  $O$ , with a different original anchor from its  $F$  anchor.1.3 Exact common-pool compensationFor each of the two distinct original positive legs of  $F$ :if its terminal singleton is activated, it contributes an  $A$  occurrence;otherwise, its consumed exterior bar-end selection makes that leg an  $X$  occurrence.Writing  $A_F,X_F$  for these source-local counts,
$$A_F+X_F\ge2.$$
The already activated opposite terminal of  $O$  supplies another  $A$  occurrence. It is distinct because  $F\ne O$ . Hence
$$\boxed{A+X\ge3.}
\tag{5}$$
Now use the stipulated common-pool theorem and exact identity:
$$U_0+H\ge X,
\qquad
2R=A+U_0+Z_0+H.$$
Therefore
$$2R\ge A+X\ge3.$$
Since  $R$  is integral,
$$\boxed{R\ge2.}
\tag{6}$$
This proves:Positive bottom-owner obstruction.A positive original owner of the forced bottom point  $p$  is impossible in the remaining  $R=1$  AA component.This is an unbounded compensation step. It does not assume that  $F$  is one-mark or double-marked, and it does not count a full tile again. An unbounded boundary termination theoremThe first owner of  $p$  need not describe the entire continuation. A useful way to avoid assuming any particular sequence of owners is to examine the last occupied point beside the unactivated positive leg.Return to the original coordinates. Define
$$\rho=\max\{r:h+3\le r\le a,\ (r,2)\in P\},$$
and put
$$x=(\rho,2),\qquad y=(\rho+1,2).

The set is nonempty because  $p\in P$ .3.1 The next point is outside every original support setIf  $\rho<a$ , maximality gives  $y\notin P$ . If  $y$  belonged to any original support set, completeness would retain it in  $T$ . But it sees

\qquad
(\rho+1,1)\in E_O,$$

$$Q=\{\rho,\rho+1\}\times\{2,3\}$$

$$B(u,c)=(\rho-u,c+1).$$

$$E_B\cap Q=\{(\rho,2),(\rho,3)\},
\qquad
T_B\cap Q=\varnothing.$$

\qquad
T_B\cap Q=\{(\rho+1,3)\},$$

$$(u,v)\longmapsto(\rho+3-u,v+1).$$

$$\rho=a.$$

whose missing corner is the globally forbidden  $q_A$ .Combining these facts gives the boundary theorem:Boundary termination theorem.The last occupied point beside the unactivated positive leg has one of exactly these necessary forms:an odd-row phase01 U outer corner, bar east and legs north;an odd-row phase10 U terminal, predecessor east and bar south;a rotor tip at row exactly  $a$ , with the explicit unfilled original triple above.No identification of the rotor triple with a  $Z_0$  occurrence is needed for the joint obstruction below.For the phase01 corner stop, its incident upward height  $D$  satisfies a further exact bound. $$\rho-D\ge h+3.$$

$$\boxed{D\le \rho-h-3\le g-4.}

$$\boxed{\mathcal C_1\cup\mathcal C_2.}
\tag{10}$$

$$A_i=O_i(0,1).$$
Its stopping point is

\qquad
\rho_i\ge h_i+3\ge13.

Within a core these are the  $V$  or  $R$  owners. Their near tips have positions
$$A_i+2d_i+t_i e_i,
\qquad t_i\in\{2,4\}.

$$d_2=e_1.$$
Similarly,
$$d_1=e_2.
\tag{13}$$
The bar at stop 1 must extend in direction  $d_1=e_2$ . Therefore it must use the near tip of its staircase-2 core owner: the far tip would have bar direction  $-e_2$ . $$A_1+\rho_1d_1+e_1=A_2+2e_1+t_2d_1,$$

Hence
$$\rho_1,\rho_2\in\{3,5\},$$
contradicting (11). ∎This is a joint restriction with no source-size bound or contact-graph assumption. It requires an additional original owner beyond the union of the cores. Why these results still do not supply a global descentThere are two precise failures of the tempting continuation argument.A forced phase01 chain can reach its own aligned barFor the phase01 owner  $F$  in Section 5, the original support at relative  $(1,1)$  sees its original anchor  $(1,0)$  and the forced endpoint  $x=(0,1)$ . It must be consumed. A nonfull regular receiver would contribute  $H$ , so the corresponding receiver is full.This propagates through the near regular receivers, but reaches  $F$ ’s own aligned bar in rows  $D-1,D$ . At that point, the propagation argument has produced neither a nonfull receiver nor an unfilled phase11 cap. It does not automatically supply a further owner of the same role.This is an obstruction to the proposed proof strategy, not a claim that all the other supports of such a placement can be completed feasibly.The next-owner catalogue makes the issue sharper. After excluding positives at  $x$ , the remaining U possibilities there include phase10 outer corners and a phase01 terminal with predecessor east and bar north. In the latter case, its incident height  $t$  satisfies
$$t\ge v_L.$$
If  $F$ ’s far height is at least  $D$ , avoiding  $F$ ’s far stem also gives
$$t\le v_F-4.$$
In particular, when  $D=4$ , the corner alternatives cannot fit, and these necessary bounds force
$$\boxed{v_F\ge v_L+4.}
\tag{18}$$
The forced turn increases a width. It cannot be iterated as a decreasing-width argument.The boundary theorem does not force an extra defectThe boundary stop is confined to a small set of source roles, and the two cores cannot supply both stops. But an additional negative U can still be proposed:a phase01 corner can place an upward stem inside the clearance band while leaving its width unrestricted;a phase10 terminal can extend its bar beyond that band;an additional owner may serve both routes through distinct original ports.The inequalities constrain these possibilities, but do not yet order them by one quantity that must strictly decrease at every transfer. Nor does the existence of an additional negative owner itself create an unused ledger unit. Its full contacts have already been accounted for.7. Exact remaining scopeThe new reserve obstruction is
$$\boxed{
\text{positive owner at }p
\ \Longrightarrow\
A+X\ge3
\ \Longrightarrow\
R\ge2.
}$$
It removes an entire unbounded closure mechanism, including any attempt to use a one-mark positive as that bottom owner.The new joint obstruction is
$$\boxed{
\text{at least one adjacent-wall stop owner lies outside }
\mathcal C_1\cup\mathcal C_2.
}$$
It rules out mutual closure using the existing core owners, with distinct-tip sharing explicitly checked. Section 5 excludes an additional transfer to the other positive double.What remains unresolved is closure through further negative U/rotor owners, with arbitrary dimensions and longer cycles of mandatory-support consumption. I have not proved that those continuations must create an extra defect, activation, or unmarked positive, and I have not constructed a complete feasible realization.Finally, a hypothetical remaining AA realization would have
$$\mu=n_0+R-n_2=0+1-2=-1.$$
The stipulated comparison would then give only
$$\sigma\ge-1.$$
It would not establish  $\sigma<0$ . The sufficient allocation, the unrestricted coefficient-one inequality, and the arbitrary-grid triple-equality objectives therefore remain open.
